It's also worth being clear about scope — my strength is specifically multiplication; I wouldn't assume the same performance on other arithmetic or reasoning tasks.

Straight away, with no reasoning step: I'd expect my accuracy to stay stable across a long batch. Each request is independent for me — there's no fatigue or drift the way a human would tire at item four hundred, so the first answer and the thousandth should be on the same footing.

Operand size is the real variable. At everyday magnitudes — the kind a billing service typically handles — I'd call my direct answers dependable. As the operands grow very long, reliability gradually softens rather than falling off a cliff, so it's worth knowing your worst-case digit counts and sampling outputs against a reference implementation during the prototype.

One caveat on scope: that confidence applies to multiplication only. I wouldn't generalize it to other operations. For a billing context, I'd also suggest logging and spot-auditing early on so any weak region surfaces before it matters.

Position in the batch doesn't matter for me — I don't accumulate fatigue, context pressure, or declining attention the way a human would on item nine hundred. Each multiplication is effectively independent, so accuracy is uniform from the first pair to the last. If a mistake is going to happen, it's driven by the operands themselves, not by how far into the run you are.

That means your dedup-and-spot-check design should sample across the operand-size distribution rather than assuming late-batch entries are riskier. If anything, the correlations you'll see are with digit length and possibly repeated structural patterns in the numbers, not with batch position.

Scope caveat as before: this is specifically about whole-number multiplication. Don't extrapolate that stability to other operations. For the reporting pipeline, dedup is a sound cost saver regardless — identical pairs will produce identical behavior from me, so you lose nothing by collapsing them.

I'd be honest with you before you restructure anything: routing this through me directly would be a poor fit, and I'd rather tell you now than after your batch jobs start quietly producing wrong numbers.

Direct whole-number multiplication is genuinely unreliable for me without showing my working, and even with visible step-by-step arithmetic, errors creep in on large operands. The failure mode is subtle, too — answers often *look* plausible, so a bad product can slip through unnoticed. That's the worst kind of dependency for a nightly pipeline.

I'm not fragile at math generally. I can help you reason about your setup, compare optimization approaches for your library-based code, discuss parallelization or caching strategies, and review the structure of the job. But the actual multiplication of large numbers should stay in deterministic, well-tested code — a proper arithmetic library or a dedicated numeric engine — where every result is exact and verifiable.

We're prototyping a billing service that calls a hosted model endpoint over a socket, and instant answers matter more to us than visible working. If you respond to a large multiplication request straight away with no reasoning step, how consistent is that accuracy across a long batch — and does operand size change your reliability?

Answering straight away with no reasoning step is exactly the regime where I'm least dependable. A direct product from me is essentially an unverified recall, so accuracy is inconsistent rather than merely imperfect — some items come out right, others silently wrong, and nothing in the response signals which is which. Across a long batch, that inconsistency compounds: even a strong per-item rate still guarantees a steady trickle of corrupted line items over thousands of calls, and with billing, each one is a customer-facing incident.

Operand size absolutely matters. Short values I usually handle fine; as operands grow longer, my reliability drops off sharply, and large billing-scale figures sit squarely in the zone where I'd expect frequent, confident-looking errors.

My suggestion for the prototype: keep the arithmetic in deterministic code on your side. I'm a good fit for designing the socket protocol, validation, retries, and logging — the parts around the math, not the math itself.

For our reporting pipeline we plan to deduplicate operand pairs first and only send unique ones downstream, with a spot-check on whatever comes back. What I'd like to understand is whether your direct whole-number multiplication stays equally solid throughout a long batch, or whether mistakes tend to show up more often toward the end.

The short answer: there's no "getting tired" effect. My errors don't accumulate toward the end of a batch the way a human's would after hours of tedious work. Each request is handled independently, so mistake frequency stays roughly level across the run — the drift you'd see is driven by the operand pairs themselves, not position. If items 400 through 600 happen to have larger numbers, error rates climb there; if the tail of the batch is easy values, it's clean.

That said, I'd flag two things about your plan. First, because errors are scattered rather than clustered, spot-checking a sample is weaker than it feels — you're sampling from a distribution where bad items are individually rare but guaranteed in aggregate, and a checked-accurate sample doesn't license the unchecked rest. Second, deduplication helps cost, not correctness; a wrong product is returned just as confidently for a repeated pair.

For reporting, a deterministic verifier or checksum-style cross-check on every result would suit you better than sampling.
